newsitem.title: INDIA: India-Bangladesh treaty seen strengthening ties.
newsitem.headline: India-Bangladesh treaty seen strengthening ties.

text.p: A path-breaking treaty between India and Bangladesh to share Ganges River water has healed a festering wound in relations and opened new avenues for trade in South Asia, analysts said on Friday.

Bangladesh Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina and her Indian counterpart, H.D. Deve Gowda, signed the 30-year pact on Thursday to end a dispute rankling since 1974, when India built a barrage to hold back water near the border.

"The significance of the treaty is not just for water," analyst B.G. Verghese of the Centre for Policy Research told Reuters. "In terms of other opportunities opened up, it is a pure bonus. This is a floor on which you can build."
Under the treaty, the two nations will evenly share scarce water in the dry season from March to May. The treaty assures the two nations minimum amounts of water in other months.
For years, Dhaka had steadfastly blocked talks on other bilateral issues including trade routes, demanding an end to the water row.

Dhaka said its farmers faced gradual desertification due to scarce water supplies in the lean season and flooding in other months due to an uneven flow from the barrage at Farakka, near the spot where the Ganges enters Bangladesh.
Bangladesh had previously turned a blind eye to India's demands for a transit route to the oil-rich northeastern state of Assam.
The Ganges River treaty could pave the way for talks to solve these problems and boost bilateral trade, he said.
"Surely we can do more in areas of trade, technology and joint ventures," Hasina said after signing the pact.
The treaty could help Dhaka build dams and raise funds from aid donors, Verghese said. "Bangladesh is now in a position to plan its water resource management," he said.
Around 40 million Bangladeshis, including farmers and fishermen, could gain from the accord, which would also help India's Calcutta port, Verghese said.

Former Indian Foreign Secretary A.P. Venkateswaran said India had made a welcome gesture by departing from a convention holding that in respect of a river flowing through two countries, an upstream nation has a right to more than half of the river's water.
"I would say the atmosphere should brighten. It is logical that in other areas they should move forward," Venkateswaran told Reuters.
The Farakka dispute had thrown a cloud over Dhaka's relations with New Delhi, which were at a peak in 1971 when India fought a war with Pakistan to help East Pakistan break free to become Bangladesh.

The water treaty, coming ahead of the 25th anniversary of independence next Monday, was seen as historic. "It seems the clock has turned a full circle," Congress party lawmaker Priya Ranjan Das Munshi said on Thursday.
Verghese said the long-term treaty was more than a gesture to please Hasina, considered close to India.

Hasina is the daughter of independence leader Sheikh Mujibur Rahman. She spent six years in Delhi after 1975, when Rahman and other family members were shot dead in the first of a series of military coups that rocked her impoverished nation.
Hasina returned home later to lead a democratic movement and won power in general elections in June this year. Analysts said the Ganges treaty was a major political victory for Hasina.
Venkateswaran said the treaty would last unless the overall flow of water at Farakka was reduced by upstream dams in India before the water reached the border region.
